power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=.119 ", "p=.249", "p=.119", "p=.249" ), Sentence = c("The Mann-Whitney U statistic was 3,244, with raw p=.119 and Holm-adjusted p=.249.", "The Mann-Whitney U statistic was 3,244, with raw p=.119 and Holm-adjusted p=.249.", "The funding test gives U=3,244; raw p=.119; Holm p=.249.", "The funding test gives U=3,244; raw p=.119; Holm p=.249." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: Federal small business awards from the National Institutes of Health fund neurosurgical devices and procedural technologies, but how often the specific funded capability reaches human use is unknown.
We determined how often these technologies had documented human implementation and in which settings.

Methods: We assembled a retrospective public-source cohort of technologies supported by Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer awards from fiscal years 2005-2020 by keyword filtering and funded-purpose review.
Confirmation required livinghuman use of the funded capability or a supported direct extension after a qualifying sametechnology award, with public evidence by October 8, 2026.
Exploratory comparisons examined program, observed phase, award era, and cumulative support.
A 500-family random sample assessed screening omissions.
Results: The cohort comprised 209 technologies, 221 award families, and 453 applications receiving $206,825,343.
Human implementation was documented for 31/209 technologies (14.8%; Wilson 95% confidence interval, 10.7%-20.3%); evidence was not located for 156 and was indeterminate for 22.
Confirmed settings were neurosurgical-scope care (26), other clinical care (2), mixed surgical cohorts (1), and nonclinical human evaluation (2).
Confirmation was more frequent with observed Phase II support than Phase I only (21/98 vs 10/111; difference, 12.4 percentage points; company-component bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 2.8-22.4).
None NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
of four conventional tests met a Holm-adjusted .05 threshold.
Screening scenarios estimated 40-76 omitted families.
Conclusion: Approximately one in seven included technologies had documented human implementation.
Linking individual awards to implemented capabilities provides an empirical benchmark for early neurosurgical translation and a practical foundation for tracking subsequent clinical evaluation.
Human implementation establishes that a capability developed in the laboratory has been exercised in a living person, allowing its clinical performance to be studied.

The IDEAL and IDEAL-D frameworks locate early human evaluation within a staged process extending through comparative assessment and long-term surveillance. [7, 16] Tracking human implementation shows which technological approaches have reached human evaluation and where further evidence is needed.
text.formatted: The IDEAL and IDEAL-D frameworks locate early human evaluation within a staged process extending through comparative assessment and long-term surveillance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16]</ref> Tracking human implementation shows which technological approaches have reached human evaluation and where further evidence is needed.

text.text: Research on translation has followed promising basic-science discoveries into clinical trials and licensed use. [3] Within neurosurgery, patent and publication analyses characterize innovation activity, while studies applying IDEAL assess the quality and sequence of evaluation. [4, 9, 15] The NIH Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs offer an additional starting point: awards identify a proposed capability, its intended purpose, and the organization developing it. [12] National assessments and linkeddatabase evaluations have examined commercialization, patents, and organizational outcomes, [10, 14] and recent neurosurgical research has mapped R01 funding among neurosurgeonscientists. [13] Linking each funded capability to human use shows whether it reached human evaluation.
text.formatted: Research on translation has followed promising basic-science discoveries into clinical trials and licensed use. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> Within neurosurgery, patent and publication analyses characterize innovation activity, while studies applying IDEAL assess the quality and sequence of evaluation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15]</ref> The NIH Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs offer an additional starting point: awards identify a proposed capability, its intended purpose, and the organization developing it. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref> National assessments and linkeddatabase evaluations have examined commercialization, patents, and organizational outcomes, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14]</ref> and recent neurosurgical research has mapped R01 funding among neurosurgeonscientists. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref> Linking each funded capability to human use shows whether it reached human evaluation.

text.text: We used the technology as the unit of assessment.
A company can hold several awards and develop related platforms with different mechanisms, delivery routes, and intended applications.
Linking awards to the capability actually implemented makes it possible to follow a specific development pathway as products evolve.
It also accommodates a funded neurosurgical capability that first reaches human evaluation in another clinical setting.
Publication-defined surgical-device cohorts provide a precedent for tracing this transition, [5] while award-defined cohorts connect the transition to a documented research investment.
text.formatted: Publication-defined surgical-device cohorts provide a precedent for tracing this transition, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> while award-defined cohorts connect the transition to a documented research investment.

text.text: We evaluated neurosurgical technologies supported by NIH SBIR/STTR awards in fiscal years 2005-2020.
Our primary objective was to estimate the proportion with qualifying public evidence of human implementation by October 8, 2026.
We described the settings of confirmed implementation and explored associations with award characteristics.
We also assessed potential screening omissions.
We distinguished technologies without qualifying evidence from those with a specific unresolved question about the evidence.
We conducted a retrospective cohort study using NIH RePORTER award records and public implementation evidence.

We retrieved fiscal-year 2005-2020 R41/R42/R43/R44 records through the RePORTER API, partitioned by year, activity code, and 25 NIH institutes/centers. [11] Acquisition yielded 29,658 applications representing 15,732 award families.
text.formatted: We retrieved fiscal-year 2005-2020 R41/R42/R43/R44 records through the RePORTER API, partitioned by year, activity code, and 25 NIH institutes/centers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> Acquisition yielded 29,658 applications representing 15,732 award families.

text.text: We applied keyword filters to project titles, abstracts, and public-health-relevance text to identify candidates for funded-purpose review.
Initial filtering flagged 3,336 families and filtered out 12,396; subsequent review and recovery established the study cohort.
Supplementary Methods S1 lists the filter terms and acquisition settings.
We used application identifiers, project numbers, recipient names, budget dates, and award amounts to link and characterize the records.

Reporting followed applicable STROBE domains. [17] Eligibility covered cranial or spinal intervention, neurovascular intervention, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)/shunt or brain-directed neurocritical procedural management, neural repair interfaces, and implanted/percutaneous pain interfaces.
text.formatted: Reporting followed applicable STROBE domains. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref> Eligibility covered cranial or spinal intervention, neurovascular intervention, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)/shunt or brain-directed neurocritical procedural management, neural repair interfaces, and implanted/percutaneous pain interfaces.

text.text: Specifically funded adjuncts and manufacturing capabilities integral to these procedures were eligible.
Funded purpose and procedural capability determined scope, including relevant peripheral nerve and pain procedures performed across specialties.
Generic neurological benefit, systemic resuscitation, generic cell manufacturing, and disease modeling alone were insufficient.
Supplementary Methods S1 details the scope rules.
We deduplicated applications by exact identifier and grouped them into technologies when the documentation supported a common mechanism and intended capability.
Mixed-purpose families were allocated at application level.
Eight families with unresolved eligibility were held outside the cohort.
Figure 1 summarizes cohort assembly and screening dispositions.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> summarizes cohort assembly and screening dispositions.

text.text: Figure 2 shows implementation classifications and settings.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> shows implementation classifications and settings.

text.text: Figure S1 presents the separate exclusionframe audit, which assesses omissions in the same 15,732-family universe after removing 378 previously covered families, leaving a 15,354-family audit frame.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref> presents the separate exclusionframe audit, which assesses omissions in the same 15,732-family universe after removing 378 previously covered families, leaving a 15,354-family audit frame.

text.text: This frozen frame includes 21 families subsequently represented in the final cohort.

Confirmation required actual use of the funded capability or a supported direct extension in a living human after a qualifying same-technology award, with supporting public evidence available by October 8, 2026.
Primary clinical reports, informative primary conference reports, and posted trial results could establish exposure.
Regulatory authorization, sponsor claims, and registry status alone were insufficient.
Animal, cadaver, specimen-only, and stored-data-only evaluations were excluded.
Other-specialty clinical use and nonclinical human evaluation qualified when they exercised the funded capability.

We searched PubMed/Europe PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov, primary reports, and supporting public sources using grant identifiers, product names, supported aliases, company names, and mechanism-specific terms.
We assessed capability identity, human exposure, and chronology together.
Later retrievals, including October 14 verification searches, could establish that evidence was available by the October 8 cutoff.
Search records retained source links and the facts supporting each decision.
We classified technologies as confirmed, not located, or indeterminate.
Not located indicated no qualifying evidence and no concrete unresolved material lead after the documented searches.
Indeterminate indicated a specific unresolved identity, chronology, or exposure fact that could change classification.
All three groups remained in the primary denominator.
We assigned confirmed technologies to four mutually exclusive settings: neurosurgical-scope care, other clinical care, mixed surgical cohorts, or nonclinical human evaluation.
One author performed evidence verification and review, with source identification and vetting assistance from a second author.
Tables S5-S7 document confirming evidence, indeterminate endpoints, and eligibility holds.
text.formatted: Tables <ref type="table">S5-S7</ref> document confirming evidence, indeterminate endpoints, and eligibility holds.

text.text: We compared any STTR support, including both-program technologies, with SBIR only; any observed Phase II application (R42/R44) with Phase I only; and earliest included fiscal year 2005-2012 with 2013-2020.
Cumulative support summed deduplicated qualifying application amounts in nominal US dollars.
Observation opportunity extended from the earliest valid included budget start to the evidence cutoff.
A separately verified earlier same-technology award could establish qualifying implementation chronology.
Missing amounts and invalid or missing dates were not imputed.
We calculated the confirmed proportion among all included technologies with a Wilson 95% confidence interval (CI). [18] Exploratory categorical comparisons used two-sided Fisher exact tests.
text.formatted: We calculated the confirmed proportion among all included technologies with a Wilson 95% confidence interval (CI). <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref> Exploratory categorical comparisons used two-sided Fisher exact tests.

text.text: Cumulative support was compared between confirmed technologies and the combined notlocated/indeterminate group using a two-sided asymptotic Mann-Whitney test with tie and continuity correction.
Holm adjustment covered the four comparisons.

Funding effect sizes were the median difference and probability of superiority, defined as the probability that support for a confirmed technology exceeded support for an unconfirmed technology, with half credit for ties.
We estimated effect-size CIs with 10,000 whole company-component bootstrap replicates per contrast, resetting NumPy PCG64 seed 20261014 for each contrast.
Technologies sharing normalized recipient identities were linked transitively, and all technologies in each sampled component were retained.
CIs used linearly interpolated percentile limits.
Wilson intervals and conventional tests assumed independent technologies; bootstrap intervals accounted for recorded shared recipients and were not multiplicity-adjusted.
Analyses used Python, NumPy, and SciPy.
Supplementary Methods S3 provides the calculation details.
We assessed potential omissions using a simple random sample without replacement of 500 families from a 15,354-family exclusion frame.
Alternative classifications of unresolved families generated eligible-frame estimates and conditional exact hypergeometric limits.
We incorporated deduplicated known recoveries and eligible families outside the cohort to estimate remaining omissions and family coverage.
Supplementary Methods S4 describes the classificationsensitivity calculations.
We also calculated a scenario in which all 22 indeterminate technologies became confirmed while the other classifications remained unchanged (Table S8).
text.formatted: We also calculated a scenario in which all 22 indeterminate technologies became confirmed while the other classifications remained unchanged (Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Institutional review board review was not required at Loyola University Chicago Stritch School of Medicine for this public-source study.
During the preparation of this work, the authors used ChatGPT (Codex, OpenAI; October 16-19, 2026) to assist with language editing and with writing analysis code.

AI tools did not independently generate content; all text, code, and analyses were directed, reviewed, edited, and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of the publication.
The cohort comprised 209 technologies, 221 award families, and 453 applications receiving $206,825,343 in nominal support (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The cohort comprised 209 technologies, 221 award families, and 453 applications receiving $206,825,343 in nominal support (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: There were 161 connected company components.
Median observation opportunity was 14.3 years (range, 6.0-21.8).
Funding amounts, valid budget starts, recipient information, and program, phase, and era classifications were complete.
Sixteen budget starts fell outside the fiscal-year boundaries of their administrative records and were retained as recorded.
One confirmed implementation preceded its earliest included budget start but followed a separately verified earlier same-technology award.
Spine surgery/reconstruction, neuro-oncology, and functional neurosurgery/epilepsy were the largest funded-purpose categories, with 32, 31, and 29 technologies, respectively (Table 1).
text.formatted: Spine surgery/reconstruction, neuro-oncology, and functional neurosurgery/epilepsy were the largest funded-purpose categories, with 32, 31, and 29 technologies, respectively (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: There were 166 SBIR-only technologies, 39 STTR-only technologies, and 4 receiving both programs.
Ninety-eight technologies had observed Phase II support and 111 had Phase I only.
Table S4 provides the complete roster.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S4</ref> provides the complete roster.

text.text: Human implementation was documented for 31/209 technologies (14.8%; Wilson 95% CI, 10.7%-20.3%).
Evidence was not located for 156/209 (74.6%) and was indeterminate for 22/209 (10.5%) (Table 2; Figure 2).
text.formatted: Evidence was not located for 156/209 (74.6%) and was indeterminate for 22/209 (10.5%) (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Among confirmed technologies, 26 (83.9%) qualified through neurosurgical-scope care, 2 (6.5%) through other clinical care, 1 (3.2%) through a mixed surgical cohort, and 2 (6.5%) through nonclinical human evaluation.
If all 22 indeterminate technologies became confirmed while the remaining classifications stayed unchanged, the proportion would be 53/209 (25.4%; Table S8).
text.formatted: If all 22 indeterminate technologies became confirmed while the remaining classifications stayed unchanged, the proportion would be 53/209 (25.4%; Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Confirmation occurred in 7/43 technologies with any STTR support and 24/166 with SBIR only (16.3% vs 14.5%; difference, 1.8 percentage points; company-component bootstrap 95% CI, -10.0 to 15.2).
Technologies with observed Phase II support had more confirmations than those with Phase I only (21/98 vs 10/111; 21.4% vs 9.0%; difference, 12.4 percentage points; 95% CI, 2.8-22.4) (Figure 3).

text.text: The corresponding raw Fisher p value was .018 and Holm-adjusted p value was .073.
Earlier-era technologies had confirmation in 21/111 compared with 10/98 later-era technologies (18.9% vs 10.2%; difference, 8.7 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.7 to 18.6).
No comparison met a Holm-adjusted .05 threshold (Table 3; Figure 3).

text.text: The median difference was $724,543 (companycomponent bootstrap 95% CI, -$131,044 to $1,458,154), and probability of superiority was 0.588 (95% CI, 0.458-0.712).
The Mann-Whitney U statistic was 3,244, with raw p=.119 and Holm-adjusted p=.249.
The 500-family sample contained 2 eligible, 497 excluded, and 1 unresolved family.
Under unresolved-excluded and unresolved-eligible scenarios, estimated remaining omissions were 40 and 76 families, corresponding to family coverage of 84.5% and 74.4%.
The combined transformed classification-sensitivity envelope was 0-248 remaining families and 47.1%-100.0% coverage (Table S2).

text.text: Human implementation was documented for approximately one in seven included NIH-funded neurosurgical technologies.
By linking individual awards to implemented capabilities, this study provides an empirical account of which technological approaches reached human evaluation and in what settings.
Each award-to-capability link connects a funding record to a specific human-use report, allowing subsequent clinical evidence for that capability to be followed.
The not-located group requires further searches for qualifying evidence.
The indeterminate group has specific unresolved facts that could change classification.
This award-defined approach complements earlier translation studies.

Contopoulos-Ioannidis and colleagues followed promising basic-science findings toward clinical trials and licensed use, [3] while Marcus and colleagues identified first-in-human reports for 24 of 205 publication-defined surgical devices (11.7%) and estimated a 9.8% probability of translation at 10 years. [5] Our cohort begins with NIH-supported capabilities and measures documented implementation through a common cutoff.
text.formatted: Contopoulos-Ioannidis and colleagues followed promising basic-science findings toward clinical trials and licensed use, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> while Marcus and colleagues identified first-in-human reports for 24 of 205 publication-defined surgical devices (11.7%) and estimated a 9.8% probability of translation at 10 years. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> Our cohort begins with NIH-supported capabilities and measures documented implementation through a common cutoff.

text.text: Starting from NIH awards also includes technologies without located human-use publications.
Linking awards and human-use reports adds a funding-based perspective to studies organized around publications, patents, or company outcomes.
The human-use reports illustrate why capability-level linkage matters.

FLoupe imaging was exercised during glioma operations, [8] and silicon-nitride spacers were implanted in the CASCADE cervical-fusion trial. [1] Multimodal scanning-fiber endoscopy was evaluated in 22 participants with Barrett's esophagus, demonstrating a clinical extension outside neurosurgical care. [2] Following the mechanism, configuration, and route of use allows a technology's development to remain traceable across changing product names and clinical indications.
text.formatted: FLoupe imaging was exercised during glioma operations, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> and silicon-nitride spacers were implanted in the CASCADE cervical-fusion trial. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> Multimodal scanning-fiber endoscopy was evaluated in 22 participants with Barrett's esophagus, demonstrating a clinical extension outside neurosurgical care. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> Following the mechanism, configuration, and route of use allows a technology's development to remain traceable across changing product names and clinical indications.

text.text: The next evaluative question is the quality of the clinical evidence generated after implementation.

Neurosurgical IDEAL reviews have shown gaps in staged evaluation: Muskens and colleagues examined the introduction of endoscopic endonasal meningioma surgery and WEB devices, [9] and Ota and colleagues found appropriate IDEAL application in only 5 of 14 primary neurosurgical papers identified in their citation review. [15] Our roster offers a complementary starting population for following funded technologies into feasibility studies, comparative trials, and longer-term assessment.
text.formatted: Neurosurgical IDEAL reviews have shown gaps in staged evaluation: Muskens and colleagues examined the introduction of endoscopic endonasal meningioma surgery and WEB devices, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> and Ota and colleagues found appropriate IDEAL application in only 5 of 14 primary neurosurgical papers identified in their citation review. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref> Our roster offers a complementary starting population for following funded technologies into feasibility studies, comparative trials, and longer-term assessment.

text.text: Retaining the distinction between clinical and nonclinical human evaluation makes that progression interpretable.
Future longitudinal studies could examine why confirmation was more frequent among technologies with observed Phase II support.
As technologies mature, they may receive laterphase support and develop clinical partnerships.
Additional documentation may also become available.
Phase II awards and cumulative funding may also occur after implementation.
A prospective study recording development stage and funding before human use could distinguish these pathways.
Here, the bootstrap interval and Holm-adjusted test summarize different inferential procedures, and the phase association remains exploratory.

Program and funding comparisons could also inform studies of development support and the organizational outcomes measured in prior NIH SBIR/STTR evaluations. [10, 14] Consistent technology identifiers could improve linkage across award records and human-use reports.
text.formatted: Program and funding comparisons could also inform studies of development support and the organizational outcomes measured in prior NIH SBIR/STTR evaluations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14]</ref> Consistent technology identifiers could improve linkage across award records and human-use reports.

text.text: Award records could carry stable product or prototype identifiers, links to earlier development awards, and dated references to human-use reports.
Investigators could specify which funded capability was exercised and the procedure in which it was used.
Trial and publication records could retain those identifiers as devices change ownership or name.
These records would make it easier to follow development across specialties and assess whether the available evidence supports further clinical study.

Human implementation, regulatory authorization, comparative benefit, and adoption would then be trackable as distinct milestones, consistent with IDEAL and IDEAL-D. [6, 7, 16] Limitations Public-source ascertainment may miss unpublished or inaccessible use, and search coverage differed among technologies.
text.formatted: Human implementation, regulatory authorization, comparative benefit, and adoption would then be trackable as distinct milestones, consistent with IDEAL and IDEAL-D. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16]</ref> Limitations Public-source ascertainment may miss unpublished or inaccessible use, and search coverage differed among technologies.

text.text: Incorrect capability linkage or chronology could also affect classification.
Some timing decisions relied on supported development sequences.
Twenty-two endpoints remained indeterminate, and screening estimates indicated potential omissions with substantial uncertainty.
The 14.8% therefore describes documented implementation in the assembled cohort rather than the full NIH portfolio.
Observation opportunity varied, and included awards were not necessarily lifetime-first support.
The broad endpoint encompasses other-specialty and nonclinical human use.
Award comparisons were exploratory and temporally ambiguous, and company components captured recorded shared recipients rather than every corporate relationship.
These features limit causal and portfolio-wide inference.
Linking NIH SBIR/STTR awards to technology-specific human evidence identified implementation for 31 of 209 included neurosurgical technologies.
This award-to-capability approach provides a benchmark for early translation and a traceable foundation for evaluating how funded technologies progress through subsequent clinical study.
